::: {.why}
Survivorship is usually discussed as missing names, but the sharper problem is the missing final return, which is concentrated exactly in the cases a strategy would have been holding.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what the correct delisting return is for a bankruptcy and for an acquisition, and why omitting it biases a long-short strategy asymmetrically.
- Bound the size of the bias for your own strategies using a stated assumption about delisting frequency and severity.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Build the bound rather than guess it: assume a delisting rate per year and a mean delisting return, both taken from published figures you cite or from a conservative assumption you state, and compute the annual drag on a long-only portfolio and on the short leg of a long-short portfolio. The two numbers differ in sign, which is the point.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Test the sensitivity of your own results: rerun the pairs strategy with a synthetic penalty applied whenever a name disappears from the universe, at three severities. Report the Sharpe at each. If the strategy dies at a plausible severity, that is a result and it belongs in milestone 5.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the limitation into reports/milestone-05-platform.md as the first entry in the list of lies your backtester tells.
:::
:::
